title: Phaethon
titleEn: The Chariot Bolts, and the Earth Burns — Metamorphoses II.111–259
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Dawn throws open her purple doors, the stars scatter, and the Sun orders the Hours to yoke his horses. Phaethon, who has already won from his father by asking the right to drive for a day, is anointed against the flame, crowned with the rays, and given a last set of instructions: spare the goad, follow the wheel-ruts, hold the middle of the road. He takes the reins gladly. The team, feeling too light a load, bolt from the track; the boy panics; the frozen constellations scorch and take fright; and at the sight of the Scorpion the reins fall from his hands. The horses drag the chariot anywhere. Mountains, cities, nations and rivers catch fire, from Athos to the Tiber.

advisory.lede: At II.235-236 the poem explains the dark skin of the peoples of Ethiopia as a mark left on their bodies by Phaethon's fire.
advisory.more: Greek and Roman writers habitually derived the look of distant peoples from the heat of the lands they lived in, and Ovid folds that theory into his narrative in two lines, attributing it to what “they believe” rather than asserting it in his own voice. What was climatic speculation then arrives now as an origin story for the body of a living people, told as damage done. The couplet stands here as Ovid wrote it; Lectorium presents the text unaltered.

sentences.t:
Dumque ea magnanimus Phaethon miratur opusque
perspicit, ecce vigil nitido patefecit ab ortu
purpureas Aurora fores et plena rosarum
atria.
sentences.l: And while great-hearted Phaethon marvels at these things and looks the work over, behold, wakeful Aurora has thrown open her purple doors from the shining east, and her halls full of roses.
sentences.n: One verb, patefecit, governs two objects across the line-break: Dawn opens both the fores, the doors, and the atria behind them. vigil, “wakeful”, is an adjective doing an adverb's work — she is awake before anyone. Notice too the tenses: the present miratur and perspicit set beside the perfect patefecit. Ovid switches between historic present and perfect constantly, and the change is nearly always a change of speed.

sentences.t:
Diffugiunt stellae, quarum agmina cogit
Lucifer et caeli statione novissimus exit.
sentences.l: The stars scatter, whose columns Lucifer gathers, and last of all he leaves his station in the sky.
sentences.i: The stars scatter in flight; Lucifer musters their columns and is the last to quit his post in the sky.
sentences.n: agmina cogere is a military idiom: the officer who cogit agmen brings up the rear of a marching column, which is exactly why Lucifer, the morning star, is novissimus, the last to go. statio is a soldier's word too, a sentry post. The whole picture of dawn is a garrison being relieved.

sentences.t:
Quem petere ut terras mundumque rubescere vidit
cornuaque extremae velut evanescere lunae,
iungere equos Titan velocibus imperat Horis.
sentences.l: And when he saw him making for the lands, and the world reddening, and the horns of the moon at her last seeming to melt away, the Titan orders the swift Hours to yoke the horses.
sentences.n: Quem opens the sentence as a connecting relative: Latin habitually starts a new sentence with a relative pronoun where English wants “and him” — here “and when he saw him making for earth”. You will meet this constantly. ut ... vidit is “when he saw”, and three accusative-and-infinitive clauses hang off it in a row. Titan is the Sun himself; the Horae, the Hours, are his stable-hands.

sentences.t:
Iussa deae celeres peragunt, ignemque vomentes,
ambrosiae suco saturos, praesepibus altis
quadrupedes ducunt adduntque sonantia frena.
sentences.l: The swift goddesses carry out the orders, and from the high stalls lead out the four-footed horses, fire-vomiting, gorged with the sap of ambrosia, and add the jangling bridles.
sentences.i: The swift goddesses do as they are told: from the high stalls they lead out the four-footed team, fire-breathing, full-fed on the sap of ambrosia, and put on the ringing bridles.
sentences.n: Word order worth watching: the two phrases describing the horses, ignem vomentes and ambrosiae suco saturos, arrive a full line before the noun they belong to, quadrupedes. Ovid holds the animals back and makes the reader see the fire and the feeding first. sonantia frena, “sounding bridles”, is the metal ringing as the bit goes in.

sentences.t:
Tum pater ora sui sacro medicamine nati
contigit et rapidae fecit patientia flammae
imposuitque comae radios, praesagaque luctus
pectore sollicito repetens suspiria dixit:
sentences.l: Then the father touched his son's face with a sacred ointment and made it able to endure the devouring flame, and set the rays upon his hair; and fetching up again and again from his troubled breast sighs that foretold grief, he said:
sentences.n: sui ... nati stands at opposite ends of its clause with the whole treatment between: Latin can separate a possessive from its noun by a line and rely on the endings to hold them together. patientia is a neuter plural adjective, “capable of enduring”, governing the genitive flammae. praesaga luctus, “foreknowing of grief”, transfers the foreboding from the father to his sighs — he already knows how this ends.

sentences.t:
“Si potes his saltem monitis parere parentis,
parce, puer, stimulis et fortius utere loris:
sentences.l: “If you can at least obey these warnings of your father: spare the goad, boy, and use the reins more strongly —
sentences.i: “If you can mind this much at least of your father's advice: go easy on the goad, boy, and lean hard on the reins.
sentences.n: utere is the imperative of the deponent utor, which takes its object in the ablative, loris — “make use of the reins”. parce takes a dative, stimulis, and means “be sparing towards the goad”, that is, leave it alone. The father has already lost the argument; the whole speech is small technical instructions offered in place of the refusal he could not make stick.

sentences.t: sponte sua properant; labor est inhibere volentes.
sentences.l: of their own accord they hurry; the work is to hold back the willing.
sentences.i: They go fast without being asked; the labour is in restraining them when they want to run.
sentences.n: volentes is a participle standing alone as a noun, “the ones that want [to go]”, where English must supply a noun or a clause. The line is built as an epigram, one half against the other: no effort to start them, all the effort in stopping them.

sentences.t:
Nec tibi directos placeat via quinque per arcus:
sectus in obliquum est lato curvamine limes,
zonarumque trium contentus fine polumque
effugit australem iunctamque aquilonibus arcton.
sentences.l: And let the road straight through the five arcs not be pleasing to you: the track is cut aslant, in a broad curve, and, content with the boundary of three zones, it shuns the southern pole and the Bear joined to the north winds.
sentences.i: And do not take a fancy to the road that runs straight through the five zones: the track is cut on a slant, in a wide curve, and, keeping inside the limit of three zones, it avoids the southern pole and the Bear that lies against the north wind.
sentences.n: placeat is a jussive subjunctive with the dative tibi — literally “let the way not be pleasing to you”, which is Latin's polite way of saying “don't choose it”. The five arcus are the zones the sky was divided into; the Sun's road cuts obliquely across them, which is why it is a curve and not a straight line. arcton, the Great Bear, keeps its Greek accusative ending in -on.

sentences.t: Hac sit iter: manifesta rotae vestigia cernes.
sentences.l: By this way let your journey be: you will see the plain tracks of the wheel.
sentences.i: Let that be your route: you will see the wheel-ruts plainly enough.
sentences.n: Hac is a bare ablative of the route taken, with via understood — Latin marks “by which way” with the ablative alone and no preposition. vestigia rotae are ruts worn into the sky by daily use, so the god is describing heaven as a country road that anyone could follow.

sentences.t:
Utque ferant aequos et caelum et terra calores,
nec preme nec summum molire per aethera currum.
sentences.l: And so that both sky and earth may bear equal heats, neither press down nor heave the chariot through the highest air.
sentences.i: And so that sky and earth get an equal share of the heat, do not bear down, and do not force the chariot up through the top of the air.
sentences.n: Utque ... ferant is a purpose clause governing both of the negative commands that follow it. preme has no object of its own — “press [it] down”, the chariot, supplied from currum in the next clause; Latin lends a noun forward and back like this freely. molire is the imperative of the deponent molior, a verb of heaving, effortful work.

sentences.t:
Altius egressus caelestia tecta cremabis,
inferius terras: medio tutissimus ibis.
sentences.l: Having gone out too high you will burn the heavenly roofs, too low, the lands: in the middle you will travel safest.
sentences.i: Go out too high and you will scorch the roofs of heaven; too low, and you burn the earth: keep to the middle and you will be safest.
sentences.n: The comparatives altius and inferius are adverbial and imply the excess by themselves — “higher [than you should]”, “lower”. In the second half terras depends on cremabis lent forward from the first half, so half a line carries a whole clause. The closing words became a proverb detached from the story: the safe course is the middle one.

sentences.t:
Neu te dexterior tortum declinet ad anguem,
neve sinisterior pressam rota ducat ad aram:
inter utrumque tene.
sentences.l: And let the wheel, too far to the right, not turn you aside towards the twisted Serpent, nor, too far to the left, lead you down to the Altar: hold between the two.
sentences.i: And don't let the wheel drift right and carry you off towards the coiled Snake, or drift left and take you down to the Altar: hold between them.
sentences.n: One subject, rota, serves both clauses and shows up only in the second. dexterior and sinisterior are comparative adjectives agreeing with it but translating as adverbs of the driver's error, “too far right”, “too far left”. Anguis (the Dragon) lies high in the north and Ara (the Altar) low in the south; pressam, “pressed down”, says that the Altar sits low on the horizon.

sentences.t:
Fortunae cetera mando,
quae iuvet et melius quam tu tibi, consulat opto.
sentences.l: The rest I entrust to Fortune; I pray that she may help, and take better thought for you than you do for yourself.
sentences.i: The rest I leave to Fortune — I only hope she helps, and looks after you better than you look after yourself.
sentences.n: quae opens as a connecting relative, “and may she”. opto governs the two subjunctives iuvet and consulat but stands last in the line, so the sentence only reveals at its very end that this has been a prayer and not a statement. consulo with the dative tibi means “take thought for”, not “consult”.

sentences.t:
Dum loquor, Hesperio positas in litore metas
umida nox tetigit.
sentences.l: While I speak, dewy Night has touched the turning-posts set on the western shore.
sentences.n: metae are the posts at the ends of a Roman racecourse that the chariots swing around; Night has just reached hers, and the sky is being described as a circus throughout this speech. Hesperio, “western”, is where her lap ends and the day's begins. The present loquor beside the perfect tetigit is the tense-shift again — the talking is still going on, the deadline has already arrived.

sentences.t:
Non est mora libera nobis:
poscimur: effulget tenebris aurora fugatis.
sentences.l: There is no delay left free to us: we are called for: the dawn blazes out, the shadows put to flight.
sentences.i: We are not free to linger: we are wanted: the dawn is blazing out and the darkness is driven off.
sentences.n: tenebris ... fugatis is an ablative absolute — a noun and a participle standing together in the ablative, self-contained, “with the shadows put to flight”, where English usually wants a clause: “now that the darkness has been driven off”. This construction is everywhere in Ovid and worth learning to see at a glance. poscimur is passive and almost impersonal: “we are being demanded”, by a world waiting for daylight.

sentences.t:
Corripe lora manu, vel, si mutabile pectus
est tibi, consiliis, non curribus utere nostris,
sentences.l: Snatch up the reins in your hand — or, if a changeable heart is yours, make use of my counsels, not my chariot,
sentences.i: Take up the reins, then — or, if you can still change your mind, take my advice instead of my chariot,
sentences.n: mutabile pectus est tibi is a dative of possession: Latin says “a changeable heart is to you” where English says “you have”. The sting of the line is in the pair of ablatives after utere, consiliis and curribus offered as though counsel and a chariot were two comparable things to make use of.

sentences.t:
dum potes et solidis etiamnunc sedibus adstas
dumque male optatos nondum premis inscius axes.
sentences.l: while you can, and while you still stand on solid ground, and while you are not yet pressing, unknowing, the axle you wished for to your own harm.
sentences.i: while you still can, while your feet are still on solid ground, and before you have put your ignorant weight on an axle it was ruin to ask for.
sentences.n: male optatos, literally “ill-wished-for”, is the poem's own verdict slipped into the father's mouth: the wish was granted, and the granting is the disaster. inscius, “not knowing”, agrees with the boy but does an English adverb's work, “unwittingly”. premis is present tense for a moment that has not arrived yet, which is why the whole sentence still feels stoppable.

sentences.t: Quae tutus spectes, sine me dare lumina terris!”
sentences.l: Which you may look at in safety — let me be the one to give the lands their light!”
sentences.i: Let me give the earth its light, and you can watch it from somewhere safe!”
sentences.n: The relative clause quae ... spectes stands in front of the noun it depends on, lumina, and its subjunctive is one of purpose: “light for you to look at, in safety”. Opening with a relative pronoun is the same connecting habit met above. sine is the imperative of sino, “allow”, taking the accusative and infinitive me dare.

sentences.t:
Occupat ille levem iuvenali corpore currum,
statque super manibusque datas contingere habenas
gaudet et invito grates agit inde parenti.
sentences.l: He takes possession of the light chariot with his young body, and stands over it, and rejoices to touch the reins given into his hands, and thereupon gives thanks to his unwilling father.
sentences.i: He takes the light chariot for his own with his boy's body, stands up in it, delights to have the reins put into his hands to hold — and thanks his unwilling father for them.
sentences.n: levem sits where a reader takes it as praise of the workmanship; a dozen lines on it becomes the cause of everything, because the car is too light for the horses to feel. invito parenti is a dative of the person, and it is doing all the cruelty in the sentence: the gratitude is aimed at a father who never wanted this. Magnus prints datas habenas, “the reins given [him]”; some editions print leves, repeating “light” a second time in three lines.

sentences.t:
Interea volucres Pyrois et Eous et Aethon,
Solis equi, quartusque Phlegon, hinnitibus auras
flammiferis implent pedibusque repagula pulsant.
sentences.l: Meanwhile the flying Pyrois and Eous and Aethon, the Sun's horses, and Phlegon the fourth, fill the airs with flame-bearing whinnyings and beat the barriers with their hooves.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the winged Pyrois, Eous and Aethon, the Sun's horses, and Phlegon the fourth, fill the air with fiery neighing and hammer the starting-gates with their hooves.
sentences.n: The four names are Greek and each of them says what its horse is: fire, dawn, blaze, burning. flammiferis has been transferred from the horses' mouths to the whinnying itself, so that the noise is what catches fire. repagula are the bars of the starting-boxes at the racecourse — the same circus imagery as the metae in the father's speech.

sentences.t:
Quae postquam Tethys, fatorum ignara nepotis
reppulit, et facta est inmensi copia caeli,
sentences.l: And after Tethys, ignorant of her grandson's fates, pushed these back, and free run of the measureless sky was made,
sentences.i: And once Tethys, knowing nothing of what was fated for her grandson, had pushed them back, and the measureless sky lay open,
sentences.n: Quae is another connecting relative, picking up repagula from the sentence before: “and after Tethys pushed these back”. fatorum ignara nepotis puts the adjective inside its own genitive phrase, “unaware of her grandson's fates”, and the arrangement is the point — the one who opens the gate is the one who does not know. copia is “an abundance” and so “unrestricted access”, with the genitive caeli.

sentences.t:
corripuere viam pedibusque per aera motis
obstantes scindunt nebulas pennisque levati
praetereunt ortos isdem de partibus Euros.
sentences.l: they seized the road, and with their feet moving through the air they cut through the clouds that stand in their way, and, lifted on wings, they pass the East winds risen from the same quarters.
sentences.i: they snatched up the road, and with hooves striking through the air they slice the clouds that block them, and, borne up on their wings, they overtake the East winds that rose from the same quarter.
sentences.n: corripuere is the poetic third-plural perfect, the short form of corripuerunt: wherever a verb ends -ere where you expect -erunt, this is what it is, and Ovid reaches for it constantly. pedibus ... motis is another ablative absolute. The perfect corripuere then hands over to the present scindunt — the tense-change is the horses getting up to speed.

sentences.t:
Sed leve pondus erat, nec quod cognoscere possent
Solis equi, solitaque iugum gravitate carebat;
sentences.l: But the weight was light, and not of a kind the Sun's horses could recognise, and the yoke lacked its accustomed heaviness;
sentences.i: But the load was light — not a weight the Sun's horses could recognise — and the yoke was without its usual burden.
sentences.n: nec quod ... possent is a relative clause of characteristic: the subjunctive turns quod into “not the kind of weight that they could…” rather than a plain “which they could not”. careo takes the ablative, gravitate. Everything that follows in the poem comes out of this one small physical fact.

sentences.t:
utque labant curvae iusto sine pondere naves
perque mare instabiles nimia levitate feruntur,
sic onere adsueto vacuus dat in aera saltus
succutiturque alte similisque est currus inani.
sentences.l: and as curved ships lurch without their proper weight, and are carried unsteady over the sea from too much lightness, so the chariot, empty of its accustomed load, gives leaps into the air and is tossed up high and is like an empty one.
sentences.i: and as ships with curved hulls wallow when they lack their proper ballast and go unsteadily over the sea from being too light, so the chariot, empty of the load it is used to, throws itself into the air, is flung high, and behaves as though nothing were in it.
sentences.n: A formal simile on the epic pattern, ut ... sic, with the comparison laid out before the thing compared. iusto sine pondere is “without a just weight”, the ballast a hull is built to carry, and nimia levitate is an ablative of cause. The last clause is the sting: similis inani, “like an empty thing”, which is nearly literally true, since the boy weighs almost nothing.

sentences.t:
Quod simulac sensere, ruunt tritumque relinquunt
quadriiugi spatium, nec quo prius ordine currunt.
sentences.l: As soon as they felt this, the four-horse team rush, and abandon the worn track, and do not run in the order they did before.
sentences.i: The moment they feel it, the team of four bolt, leave the beaten track, and no longer keep the order they ran in before.
sentences.n: Quod is the connecting relative again, this time as object of sensere — another -ere perfect for -erunt. tritum ... spatium, “the rubbed-away space”, is the track polished smooth by daily driving. quadriiugi, “the four-yoked ones”, is simply the noun for a team of four. And again the perfect gives way instantly to the present ruunt: the bolt happens while we watch.

sentences.t:
Ipse pavet nec qua commissas flectat habenas,
nec scit, qua sit iter; nec, si sciat, imperet illis.
sentences.l: He himself is terrified, and neither knows which way to turn the reins entrusted to him, nor where the road is; nor, should he know, would he command them.
sentences.i: The boy himself is in a panic: he does not know which way to pull the reins put into his hands, nor where the road runs — and if he did know, he could not control them.
sentences.n: scit is held back into the second line and serves the clause in front of it as well as the one behind: “he neither knows how to turn the reins ... nor knows where the road is”. si sciat ... imperet has the present subjunctive in both halves — “should he come to know, he still would not command them” — so knowledge is left open as a possibility and then made not to matter. The line ends on illis, the horses, who are now the ones deciding.

sentences.t:
Tum primum radiis gelidi caluere triones
et vetito frustra temptarunt aequore tingi,
sentences.l: Then for the first time the icy plough-oxen grew hot with the rays and tried in vain to be dipped in the forbidden sea,
sentences.i: Then for the first time the frozen Wagon-oxen grew warm in the rays and tried, in vain, to be dipped in a sea forbidden them,
sentences.n: triones are the plough-oxen, the stars of the Bear, which for anyone watching from the Mediterranean never set. vetito aequore is precisely that: they are not permitted to go under the horizon, which is why they cannot cool off. temptarunt is a syncopated perfect for temptaverunt, the same shortening habit as the -ere forms, and very common in verse.

sentences.t:
quaeque polo posita est glaciali proxima serpens,
frigore pigra prius nec formidabilis ulli,
incaluit sumpsitque novas fervoribus iras.
sentences.l: and the Serpent, which is set nearest to the icy pole, sluggish before with cold and frightening to nobody, grew hot and took on new rages from the burning.
sentences.i: and the Snake that lies nearest the frozen pole, slow with cold before and no threat to anyone, grew hot and took on a fresh temper from the heat.
sentences.n: The noun sits inside its own relative clause: quae ... serpens is “the serpent, which…”, an order Latin allows and English cannot copy. formidabilis takes a dative of the person threatened, ulli. The whole couplet turns on temperature as a joke — the cold was what kept it harmless, and the heat gives it a personality.

sentences.t:
Te quoque turbatum memorant fugisse, Boote,
quamvis tardus eras et te tua plaustra tenebant.
sentences.l: You too, Boötes, they relate, fled in confusion, although you were slow and your own wagon was holding you back.
sentences.i: You too, Boötes, they say, bolted in confusion, slow as you were, and held back by your own wagon.
sentences.n: Ovid breaks off the narrative to speak to a character directly — apostrophe, marked here by the vocative Boote. He does it repeatedly through the poem, and it is a way of standing close to what he describes without narrating it. memorant, “they relate”, is an impersonal “the story goes” that keeps the poet's own credit out of it. Boötes is the Ox-driver, the constellation walking behind the plough-oxen of the line above, and the plaustrum is the wagon they drag.

sentences.t:
Ut vero summo despexit ab aethere terras
infelix Phaethon penitus penitusque iacentes,
palluit et subito genua intremuere timore,
suntque oculis tenebrae per tantum lumen obortae.
sentences.l: But when unhappy Phaethon looked down from the highest air at the lands lying far and far below, he went pale, and his knees shook with sudden fear, and darkness rose over his eyes through so much light.
sentences.i: But when poor Phaethon looked down from the height of the upper air at the earth lying far, far beneath him, he turned white, his knees shook with sudden terror, and through all that blaze of light a darkness came up over his eyes.
sentences.n: penitus penitusque, one adverb doubled with -que, is the distance itself: “deep, and deep down”. intremuere is another -ere perfect. The last line is the whole point of the passage: tenebrae obortae, “shadows risen up”, planted inside per tantum lumen, “through so great a light” — he blacks out in the brightest place there is.

sentences.t:
Et iam mallet equos numquam tetigisse paternos,
iam cognosse genus piget et valuisse rogando,
sentences.l: And now he would rather never have touched his father's horses; now it irks him to have found out his parentage, and to have prevailed by asking,
sentences.i: And now he would rather he had never laid a hand on his father's horses; now he is sick of having learnt whose son he was, and of having got his way by asking,
sentences.n: mallet is a subjunctive of unfulfilled wish, “he would rather”, with the perfect infinitive tetigisse for the thing that cannot now be undone. piget is impersonal — “it disgusts” — and takes the person in the accusative with infinitives for what disgusts him. rogando is a gerund in the ablative, “by asking”: the means by which he won, which is the thing he now regrets.

sentences.t:
iam Meropis dici cupiens ita fertur, ut acta
praecipiti pinus borea, cui victa remisit
frena suus rector, quam dis votisque reliquit.
sentences.l: now, wanting to be called the son of Merops, he is carried as a ship is driven by a headlong north wind, whose own helmsman has let the beaten reins go and left her to the gods and to prayers.
sentences.i: now, wishing he could be called the son of Merops, he is swept along like a ship driven by a headlong north wind, whose helmsman has let the beaten steering go and abandoned her to the gods and to prayer.
sentences.n: Meropis is a bare genitive with the noun understood — “to be called [the son] of Merops”, the mortal he had believed was his father before the whole business began. ita ... ut sets up the simile, and pinus, “pine”, stands for the ship by the wood it is built of. Notice that Ovid keeps the chariot's own vocabulary inside the sea-image, frena for the steering, so that the two wrecks become one.

sentences.t:
Quid faciat? multum caeli post terga relictum,
ante oculos plus est!
sentences.l: What is he to do? Much of the sky is left behind his back, more is before his eyes!
sentences.i: What is he to do? A great stretch of sky lies behind him, and more of it ahead!
sentences.n: faciat is a deliberative subjunctive: not “what does he do” but “what is he to do”, the question a person puts to himself when there is no answer. est serves both halves of the sentence, and relictum agrees with multum. The whole thought is measured out as space, behind the back and in front of the eyes, which is how he will think from here on.

sentences.t:
animo metitur utrumque,
et modo quos illi fatum contingere non est,
prospicit occasus, interdum respicit ortus:
sentences.l: he measures both in his mind, and now he looks ahead to the settings, which it is not his fate to reach, at times he looks back at the risings:
sentences.i: he measures both in his mind: now he looks ahead to the west, which it is not his fate to reach, and now he looks back to the east.
sentences.n: quos ... contingere non est works with fatum as the predicate noun and the infinitive contingere as the subject of est: “to reach which is not [his] fate”, with illi the dative of the person it is or is not fated for. The relative clause once more stands in front of its noun, occasus. prospicit and respicit, the forward look and the backward, divide the line as they divide his position.

sentences.t:
quidque agat ignarus stupet et nec frena remittit
nec retinere valet nec nomina novit equorum.
sentences.l: and not knowing what he is to do he is stunned, and neither lets the reins go nor is strong enough to hold them back nor knows the horses' names.
sentences.i: and, not knowing what to do, he is stupefied: he neither drops the reins nor can pull them in — and he does not even know the horses' names.
sentences.n: quid agat is an indirect deliberative question hanging on ignarus, an adjective governing a clause. The three nec clauses fall away in descending order and the last one is the humiliation: a Roman charioteer steered partly by calling to his team, so a driver who does not know their names has no voice in the matter at all.

sentences.t:
Sparsa quoque in vario passim miracula caelo
vastarumque videt trepidus simulacra ferarum.
sentences.l: Trembling, he sees also the marvels scattered here and there over the dappled sky, and the likenesses of huge wild beasts.
sentences.i: In his terror he sees too the wonders scattered everywhere across the dappled sky, and the shapes of enormous beasts.
sentences.n: The constellations are the miracula and the simulacra ferarum, the “likenesses of wild animals” — from where he is they have stopped being pictures. videt is held to the second line and governs both accusatives at once. trepidus is an adjective where English wants an adverb or a phrase, “in fear”; Latin prefers to describe the person rather than the manner.

sentences.t:
Est locus, in geminos ubi bracchia concavat arcus
scorpius et cauda flexisque utrimque lacertis
porrigit in spatium signorum membra duorum.
sentences.l: There is a place where the Scorpion hollows his arms into twin bows and with his tail and his limbs bent both ways stretches his body out over the space of two signs.
sentences.i: There is a place where the Scorpion curves his arms into a double bow and, with his tail and his claws bent out on either side, spreads his body across the space of two signs.
sentences.n: Est locus is a set formula for opening a description; from here Ovid stops the story to look at something. signorum ... duorum records that the Scorpion was reckoned to fill two of the zodiac's twelve places, claws and body. bracchia and lacerti are both human words — the arm, and the muscle of the upper arm — used of the claws, and that is what makes the creature horrible rather than merely large.

sentences.t:
Hunc puer ut nigri madidum sudore veneni
vulnera curvata minitantem cuspide vidit,
mentis inops gelida formidine lora remisit.
sentences.l: When the boy saw him, soaked with the sweat of black poison and threatening wounds with his curved sting, out of his mind with icy dread he let the reins go.
sentences.i: When the boy saw him — dripping with the sweat of black venom, threatening wounds with his hooked sting — he lost his mind in cold terror and let the reins go.
sentences.n: Hunc is thrown to the very front of the sentence, so the reader meets the creature before meeting the boy who is looking at it. madidum sudore veneni makes the poison something the animal perspires, wet on the outside of it. mentis inops is a genitive after an adjective of lacking, “destitute of mind”, and gelida formidine is the one cold thing in a passage that is otherwise all heat.

sentences.t:
Quae postquam summum tetigere iacentia tergum,
exspatiantur equi, nulloque inhibente per auras
ignotae regionis eunt,
sentences.l: And after these, lying slack, touched the tops of their backs, the horses go out of their bounds, and with nothing holding them they go through the airs of a region unknown to them,
sentences.i: And once the reins, hanging slack, had fallen across their backs, the horses run out of their course, and with nothing to hold them they go through the air of a country they do not know,
sentences.n: Quae is the connecting relative again, picking up lora from the line before; tetigere is another -ere perfect. nullo inhibente is an ablative absolute with barely a noun in it — “with nobody holding back” — about the tightest form the construction takes. exspatiantur is literally “they go outside the measured space”, off the marked track: the racecourse word again.

sentences.t:
quaque impetus egit,
hac sine lege ruunt altoque sub aethere fixis
incursant stellis rapiuntque per avia currum.
sentences.l: and by whatever way their own onrush drove them, by that way they rush without law, and they collide with the stars fixed under the high air and drag the chariot through pathless places.
sentences.i: and wherever their own momentum takes them, that way they run with no rule at all, crashing into the stars fixed beneath the high air and hauling the chariot through trackless country.
sentences.n: qua ... hac, “by which way ... by that way”, is a matched pair of bare ablatives of route — the same construction as Hac sit iter in the father's instructions, and the echo is deliberate: the one road he was told to keep to has become anywhere at all. avia, “places off the road”, is a word for wild country, used here of the sky.

sentences.t:
Et modo summa petunt, modo per declive viasque
praecipites spatio terrae propiore feruntur.
sentences.l: And now they make for the heights, now down the slope and along headlong roads they are carried through a space nearer to the earth.
sentences.i: Now they make for the heights, now they are swept down the slope, along plunging roads, through a space closer to the earth.
sentences.n: modo ... modo, “now ... now”, is the standard pair for alternation, and here it is doing the pitching of the chariot. declive is a neuter adjective used as a noun, “the downhill”. praecipites agrees with vias, so it is the roads that are headlong rather than the horses — a transfer of the epithet Ovid is fond of.

sentences.t:
Inferiusque suis fraternos currere Luna
admiratur equos, ambustaque nubila fumant;
sentences.l: And the Moon wonders that her brother's horses run lower than her own, and the scorched clouds smoke;
sentences.i: The Moon looks on amazed at her brother's horses running below her own — and the scorched clouds are smoking.
sentences.n: suis is an ablative of comparison after the comparative adverb inferius, with equis to be understood from the equos at the line's end: “lower than her own [horses]”. fraternos is an adjective where English wants a genitive, “her brother's”, a habit Latin keeps for close kin. admiratur takes an accusative and infinitive, equos currere.

sentences.t:
corripitur flammis ut quaeque altissima, tellus
fissaque agit rimas et sucis aret ademptis.
sentences.l: the earth is seized by the flames, each part as it is highest, and, split open, it drives cracks apart and grows dry, its juices taken away.
sentences.i: the earth catches fire, the highest ground first, splits, opens cracks, and dries out with its moisture taken from it.
sentences.n: ut quaeque altissima [est] is the idiom in which ut with a superlative means “in proportion as” — “each part, the higher it stands” — so the fire takes the high ground first. sucis ademptis is another ablative absolute. fissa is a perfect participle doing the work English would give a second finite verb: “it splits and opens cracks”.

sentences.t:
Pabula canescunt, cum frondibus uritur arbor,
materiamque suo praebet seges arida damno.
sentences.l: The pastures grow white, the tree burns along with its leaves, and the dry crop furnishes material for its own destruction.
sentences.i: The pastures go white, the tree burns leaves and all, and the parched corn supplies the fuel for its own ruin.
sentences.n: canescunt is “grow grey-white”, the colour-word for age used of grass scorched out of its colour. suo ... damno is a dative of purpose, “for its own destruction”, and it is wrapped around praebet seges arida so that the reader must hold “its own” open until damno finally arrives — the crop is both the fuel and what the fuel destroys.

sentences.t:
Parva queror: magnae pereunt cum moenibus urbes,
cumque suis totas populis incendia gentes
in cinerem vertunt.
sentences.l: I complain of small things: great cities perish with their walls, and the fires turn whole nations, with their peoples, into ash.
sentences.i: These are small things I am complaining of: great cities perish with their walls, and the fires turn whole nations, populations and all, to ashes.
sentences.n: queror is first person, and the poet steps into his own poem for one line to say that everything described so far was not worth describing. Notice the two uses of cum a line apart, both “along with”: the walls go with the cities and the peoples with the nations, so that nothing at all is left over.

sentences.t:
Silvae cum montibus ardent,
ardet Athos Taurusque Cilix et Tmolus et Oete
et tum sicca, prius creberrima fontibus, Ide,
virgineusque Helicon et nondum Oeagrius Haemus;
sentences.l: The woods burn along with the mountains; Athos burns, and Cilician Taurus, and Tmolus, and Oete, and Ide, dry then, though before that thick with springs, and virgin Helicon, and Haemus, not yet Oeagrian;
sentences.i: The woods burn with the mountains: Athos is on fire, and Cilician Taurus, Tmolus, Oeta, and Ida, dry now though it had been thick with springs before, and virgin Helicon, and Haemus, not yet Oeagrian.
sentences.n: ardent at the end of one clause and ardet at the head of the next is the fire being handed from place to place, and the catalogue runs outward from Greece across the known world. tum sicca, prius creberrima fontibus dates a fact to the moment of the story: dry then, well-watered before. nondum Oeagrius dates a word instead — the mountain has not yet acquired the epithet, and Ovid tells the reader so from inside the narrative.

sentences.t:
ardet in inmensum geminatis ignibus Aetna
Parnasusque biceps et Eryx et Cynthus et Othrys,
et tandem nivibus Rhodope caritura, Mimasque
Dindymaque et Mycale natusque ad sacra Cithaeron.
sentences.l: Aetna burns beyond measure with doubled fires, and two-peaked Parnasus, and Eryx, and Cynthus, and Othrys, and Rhodope, at last about to lose her snows, and Mimas and Dindyma and Mycale and Cithaeron, born for holy rites.
sentences.i: Etna blazes beyond measure with fires now doubled, and two-headed Parnassus, and Eryx, Cynthus, Othrys, and Rhodope, at last about to lose her snows, and Mimas, Dindyma, Mycale, and Cithaeron, born for sacred rites.
sentences.n: geminatis ignibus is the wit of the line: Etna already had a fire of its own, so this one is simply added to it. caritura is a future participle with the ablative that careo takes — “about to be without her snows”, an event held just beyond the edge of the sentence. natus ad sacra, “born for holy rites”, is said of a mountain as though of a person, and marks Cithaeron out as a place of ritual.

sentences.t:
Nec prosunt Scythiae sua frigora: Caucasus ardet
Ossaque cum Pindo maiorque ambobus Olympus
aeriaeque Alpes et nubifer Appenninus.
sentences.l: Nor do her own frosts help Scythia: Caucasus burns, and Ossa with Pindus, and Olympus greater than both, and the airy Alps and cloud-carrying Appenninus.
sentences.i: Scythia's own frosts are no help to her: the Caucasus burns, and Ossa with Pindus, and Olympus greater than the two of them, and the high Alps and the cloud-carrying Apennines.
sentences.n: prosum takes a dative of the person helped, Scythiae, and sua frigora, “her own cold”, is exactly the thing that ought to have protected her. ambobus is an ablative of comparison after maior. The catalogue is arranged to end in Italy, which is where the poem's first readers were sitting.

sentences.t:
Tum vero Phaethon cunctis e partibus orbem
adspicit accensum nec tantos sustinet aestus,
ferventesque auras velut e fornace profunda
ore trahit currusque suos candescere sentit;
sentences.l: Then indeed Phaethon sees the world set alight on every side and does not endure such heats, and draws burning air with his mouth as from a deep furnace, and feels his own chariot growing white-hot;
sentences.i: Now Phaethon sees the world alight on every side and cannot bear the heat of it; he draws burning air into his mouth as out of the depth of a furnace, and feels his own chariot glowing white.
sentences.n: orbem and accensum are split across the line-break, so the object arrives first and the participle that ruins it a beat later — a standard way of holding a shock back. candescere is inceptive: the -sc- infix means “begin to be white”, heat going past red. ore trahit, “draws with his mouth”, is what breathing has become.

sentences.t:
et neque iam cineres eiectatamque favillam
ferre potest calidoque involvitur undique fumo,
quoque eat, aut ubi sit, picea caligine tectus
nescit et arbitrio volucrum raptatur equorum.
sentences.l: and now he cannot bear the ashes and the flung-up embers, and he is wrapped on every side in hot smoke, and, covered in pitch-black murk, he does not know where he is going, or where he is, and is dragged along at the discretion of the flying horses.
sentences.i: and now he cannot endure the ash and the sparks flung up at him; he is wrapped on every side in hot smoke; and, covered in pitch-black dark, he no longer knows where he is going or where he is, and is hauled about at the horses' own discretion.
sentences.n: quo eat and ubi sit are indirect questions in the subjunctive, both depending on nescit at the head of the following line — the verb is held back so that the two lost questions come first and the not-knowing arrives last. And watch quoque here: it is quo-que, “and where to”, not the adverb “also”, a trap this poem lays often. arbitrio, “by the judgement of”, is a bitter ablative: the decisions now belong to the animals.

sentences.t:
Sanguine tum credunt in corpora summa vocato
Aethiopum populos nigrum traxisse colorem.
sentences.l: Then, they believe, with the blood called to the surface of the body, the peoples of the Ethiopians drew their black colour.
sentences.i: That was when, they believe, the blood was summoned to the surface of the body and the peoples of Ethiopia took on their black colour.
sentences.n: Sanguine ... vocato is an ablative absolute wrapped around the whole of the first line, “with the blood summoned”, and traxisse is a perfect infinitive in indirect statement after credunt. credunt is impersonal, “people believe”, and Ovid hands the explanation to those people rather than making it himself — the same distancing as memorant used of Boötes above. Greek and Roman writers standardly derived the look of far-off peoples from the climate of their country; here that theory is compressed into one event inside a story.

sentences.t:
Tum facta est Libye raptis umoribus aestu
arida, tum nymphae passis fontesque lacusque
deflevere comis: quaerit Boeotia Dircen,
Argos Amymonen, Ephyre Pirenidas undas.
sentences.l: Then Libye was made dry, her moisture snatched away by the heat; then the nymphs with loosened hair wept for their springs and their lakes: Boeotia looks for Dirce, Argos for Amymone, Ephyre for the waters of Pirene.
sentences.i: Then Libya was made a desert, her moisture torn out of her by the heat; then the nymphs, hair let down, wept for their springs and lakes: Boeotia looks for Dirce, Argos for Amymone, Ephyre for Pirene's water.
sentences.n: facta est ... arida is one predicate split over two lines with its whole cause set inside it, raptis umoribus aestu — another ablative absolute. passis ... comis, “with the hair let loose”, is the standard posture of mourning; deflevere is another -ere perfect. In the last line the single verb quaerit is lent to all three places, each of them searching for the spring that made it famous.

sentences.t:
Nec sortita loco distantes flumina ripas
tuta manent: mediis Tanais fumavit in undis
Peneusque senex Teuthranteusque Caicus
et celer Ismenos cum Phegiaco Erymantho
sentences.l: Nor do the rivers that drew by lot banks far apart in place remain safe: Tanais smoked in the middle of his waters, and old Peneus and Teuthrantean Caicus and swift Ismenos with Phegian Erymanthus
sentences.i: Nor are the rivers safe for having been allotted banks set far apart: Tanais smoked in mid-stream, and old Peneus, and Teuthrantean Caicus, and swift Ismenos with Phegian Erymanthus,
sentences.n: sortita is the perfect participle of the deponent sortior and is active in sense — the rivers “having drawn by lot” their banks, with ripas as its object — and the width of that allotment, loco distantes, is exactly what should have kept them out of one another's danger. mediis ... in undis wraps around the river's name, so Tanais is literally set in the middle of his own water. From here the catalogue of mountains becomes a catalogue of rivers.

sentences.t:
arsurusque iterum Xanthus flavusque Lycormas,
quique recurvatis ludit Maeandrus in undis.
Mygdoniusque Melas et Taenarius Eurotas.
sentences.l: and Xanthus, destined to burn a second time, and yellow Lycormas, and Maeandrus, who plays in his curling-back waters, and Mygdonian Melas and Taenarian Eurotas.
sentences.i: and Xanthus, who would burn a second time, and yellow Lycormas, and Maeandrus, playing in his doubled-back waters, and Mygdonian Melas and Taenarian Eurotas.
sentences.n: arsurus is a future participle, “about to burn”, and iterum points forward out of this poem altogether — the river will burn again in another story, and Ovid tells us so in one word. quique is the connecting relative with -que fastened to it. ludit, “plays”, is the usual verb for the Maeander's wandering, and recurvatis ... in undis bends around it the way the river does.

sentences.t:
Arsit et Euphrates Babylonius, arsit Orontes
Thermodonque citus Gangesque et Phasis et Hister.
sentences.l: Babylonian Euphrates burned too, Orontes burned, and swift Thermodon and Ganges and Phasis and Hister.
sentences.n: arsit repeated — once at the end of its clause and once at the head of the next — is the same handing-on of fire heard in ardent ... ardet in the mountains. These rivers mark the far edges of the world as Rome knew it: Mesopotamia, Syria, the Black Sea coast, India, and the Danube.

sentences.t:
Aestuat Alpheus, ripae Spercheides ardent,
quodque suo Tagus amne vehit, fluit ignibus aurum,
sentences.l: Alpheus seethes, the Spercheian banks burn, and the gold that Tagus carries in his own stream flows with the fires,
sentences.i: Alpheus boils, the banks of Spercheus burn, and the gold that Tagus carries in his stream runs molten in the flames,
sentences.n: The relative clause quod ... vehit again comes before its noun aurum, so the sentence tells you what is being carried before it tells you it is gold. fluit is exact and grim: metal that is normally carried by the water now flows on its own account. ripae Spercheides uses a Greek-style adjective made from the river's name where Latin would more often use a genitive.

sentences.t:
et quae Maeonias celebrabant carmine ripas
flumineae volucres, medio caluere Caystro.
sentences.l: and the river birds that used to fill the Maeonian banks with song grew hot in the middle of Caystrus.
sentences.i: and the river birds that used to crowd the Maeonian banks with song grew hot in mid-Cayster.
sentences.n: The relative clause once more precedes its noun, flumineae volucres, which is held back a whole line. celebrabant is imperfect, for the habit of years, and caluere — another -ere perfect — is the single moment that ends it. medio ... Caystro folds the river around the birds exactly as mediis ... in undis folded it around Tanais.

sentences.t:
Nilus in extremum fugit perterritus orbem
occuluitque caput, quod adhuc latet: ostia septem
pulverulenta vacant, septem sine flumine valles.
sentences.l: The Nile fled terrified to the world's edge and hid his head, which still lies hidden: his seven mouths lie empty and dusty, seven valleys without a river.
sentences.i: The Nile fled in terror to the edge of the world and hid his head, which is hidden to this day: the seven mouths lie empty and dusty, seven valleys with no river in them.
sentences.n: quod adhuc latet, “which even now lies hidden”, is a joke and a piece of information at once: the source of the Nile was unknown to the ancient world, and Ovid supplies a cause for the ignorance. caput is both a river's “head”, its source, and the head the personified river covers. The closing line drops the verb altogether — septem sine flumine valles — and the bareness is the effect.

sentences.t:
Fors eadem Ismarios Hebrum cum Strymone siccat
Hesperiosque amnes Rhenum Rhodanumque Padumque,
cuique fuit rerum promissa potentia, Thybrin.
sentences.l: The same chance dries the Ismarian [rivers], Hebrus with Strymon, and the western rivers, Rhenus and Rhodanus and Padus, and Thybris, to whom power over the world had been promised.
sentences.i: The same fortune dries the Ismarian streams, Hebrus and Strymon with him, and the rivers of the west, Rhine and Rhone and Po — and Tiber, to whom mastery of the world had been promised.
sentences.n: Ismarios is accusative plural and so cannot belong to the singular Hebrum beside it: it agrees with a plural noun left unexpressed — “the Ismarian [rivers]”, supplied in square brackets above — which Hebrum cum Strymone then names, exactly as Hesperios amnes in the next line is filled out by Rhenum, Rhodanum and Padum. The catalogue is arranged to finish here, on Rome's own river, and cui ... promissa potentia rerum, “to whom power over the world was promised”, turns a burning stream into the empire the poem's first readers were living in. Thybrin keeps its Greek accusative ending.
